description: I'm Mahi, lead of CUET_404. For NASA Space Apps Challenge #6, we're building Route200: the satellite data and the warnings already exist, but the route connecting them to people doesn't. We're building that route: a change-detection engine feeding a plain-language SMS/voice alert and a visual awareness experience. Looking for teammates with backend/data engineering, GIS/remote sensing, or SMS/USSD/IVR skills.
summary: Route200 is a climate-risk project by team CUET_404 for NASA Space Apps 2026, Challenge #6, "Dancing with the SARs." It turns radar satellite data into early warnings for communities in Bangladesh. One shared change-detection pipeline compares Sentinel-1 SAR amplitude across dates to map riverbank erosion along the Jamuna and landslide scars in the Chattogram Hill Tracts. Radar sees through monsoon cloud, when optical satellites fail. The results feed two tracks. The first is a public, Bangla-first web experience with an interactive risk map, real before-and-after satellite evidence for each zone, and a walkable 3D ground view built from measured terrain. The second is an alert channel that sends SMS and Bangla voice calls to households in risk zones, with no app or smartphone needed. The aim is to get satellite warnings to people on the ground before the land moves.
details:
Route200 turns radar satellite data into early warnings for people living on riverbanks and hillsides in Bangladesh. A change-detection pipeline compares Sentinel-1 SAR images from two dates and differences their backscatter to find new erosion along the Jamuna river and new landslide scars in the Chattogram Hill Tracts. Radar sees through monsoon cloud, so it works when optical satellites cannot.

The results feed two channels. The first is a public, Bangla-first web app with an interactive map of 12 named zones, a before-and-after satellite evidence page for each zone, and a walkable 3D ground view for Teknaf and Sonatola. The ground views are built from Copernicus elevation and ESA WorldCover land cover, not illustrated by hand. The second channel is an alert signup for SMS and Bangla voice calls, so households without smartphones or data plans can still be warned.

The benefit is time. The same satellite data should reach a farmer or a family before the ground gives way. The approach is deliberately simple: amplitude differencing instead of full InSAR, because it is robust under monsoon cloud and easy to check. The pipeline is written in Python (NumPy, rasterio, xarray, earthaccess). The web app uses Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind, MapLibre GL JS and Three.js, with Vitest for tests. The alert endpoint currently validates and logs signups; connecting it to a contacts database is the next step.
